name: Kavitha
definition: Kavitha is a composite portrait of a woman from Hassan's heritage-town economy, balancing government care work with tourism-linked livelihoods in the shadow of the Hoysala temples. She represents the Vokkaliga-majority plains-Malnad household navigating children's education costs, agricultural pressures and the gaps between local work and urban opportunity.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Kavitha works mornings at the anganwadi centre near Belur town, preparing midday meals and running health checks for thirty-odd children, earning around ₹8,000 a month after deductions. Three afternoons a week she helps her cousin's homestay near the Chennakeshava Temple, cleaning rooms and serving breakfast to weekend visitors from Bengaluru and foreign tourists during the cooler months, adding another ₹3,000-4,000. Her husband Manjunath owns four acres of coconut and arecanut on the Yagachi reservoir's edge, and hires labour for the two annual harvests; coconut prices have been poor the past two years, hovering near ₹25-28 per nut, and he supplements income by driving their tractor for hire during the potato season around Arsikere. Kavitha's day begins at five-thirty with rangoli, coffee and breakfast; by seven she is at the anganwadi, returning after two to cook lunch, help with homework and then leave for the homestay if the booking list demands it. Dinner is late; she is chronically tired. The dual income just about meets school fees, loan instalments and household expenses, leaving almost nothing for savings or emergencies.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Kavitha lives in a tiled house in a Belur ward with her husband, two children—Rakshitha, fourteen, in ninth standard at the government high school, and Akash, eleven, in sixth standard at a Kannada-medium aided school—and her mother-in-law, who is seventy and manages the kitchen when Kavitha is out. Manjunath's elder brother migrated to Mysuru for a printing-press job fifteen years ago and rarely visits; the land was divided then, leaving Manjunath the smaller parcel. Kavitha married at twenty-two after completing her PUC; her parents, small farmers near Channarayapatna, could not afford a college hostel fee. She had hoped to study for a BA, but the marriage came first. Her mother-in-law, though loving, holds firm ideas about ritual and propriety, and Kavitha carefully negotiates her work hours to avoid open conflict. Rakshitha is reaching an age where marriage talk surfaces among relatives, but Kavitha and Manjunath want her to finish her PUC and ideally pursue a degree; Manjunath's mother is less convinced. Akash is an eager student but struggles with English. Kavitha does most of the caregiving—her husband helps with the children's school transport but leaves cooking, cleaning and elder care to her.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Kavitha completed her SSLC at a government school in Channarayapatna taluk and her PUC in Hassan town, travelling daily by bus; she was a middling student, more interested in the arts than science, but her family lacked the means to send her further. Akash attends an aided Kannada-medium school nearby; the fees are modest—₹1,200 a year—but books, uniform and the compulsory computer class add another ₹3,000. Kavitha dreams of sending both children to a private English-medium school, but the fees—₹25,000-30,000 per child per year—are out of reach. Rakshitha wants to study commerce and become a bank officer; Kavitha and Manjunath support this, though they worry about the cost of a BCom and the need for Mysuru or Bengaluru coaching for competitive exams. Akash is less clear about his future; he enjoys drawing and talks vaguely of becoming an engineer.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Kavitha suffers from chronic lower-back pain and anaemia, diagnosed three years ago at the government taluk hospital in Belur; the doctor advised rest and iron supplements, but rest is impossible given her double work schedule, and she takes the tablets only sporadically. She delivered both children at the same hospital; Rakshitha's birth was straightforward, but Akash's involved a retained placenta and required a referral to Hassan town. Her mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure, controlled with daily medication from the government dispensary and a monthly check-up at a private clinic in Belur that charges ₹200 per visit. The family is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat, though Kavitha has never used the card; she distrusts the bureaucracy and prefers the known private doctors for anything beyond basic treatment. Manjunath had a tractor accident two years ago, fracturing his wrist; the surgery at a private hospital in Hassan cost ₹45,000, mostly borrowed, and the loan still hangs over them. Kavitha worries about Rakshitha's irregular periods and took her to a gynaecologist last year, spending ₹1,500 on scans and tablets. The anganwadi work exposes her to childhood illnesses—last monsoon she caught a flu from a child that left her bedridden for a week, and there was no paid leave. Snakebite and road accidents are constant background fears; a neighbour's son died from a viper bite in the coconut grove four years ago.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Kavitha's family are Vokkaligas, the dominant farming community in Hassan, and she participates in the cycle of Vokkaliga weddings, housewarming ceremonies and death rites that knit the neighbourhood together. She visits the Chennakeshava Temple in Belur every Thursday, circumambulating the sanctum and placing flowers, finding in the ritual a rare moment of calm; the Hoysala sculptures fill her with pride—tourists from Japan and America photograph them, and she tells Rakshitha this is their heritage. Her mother-in-law insists on strict adherence to pollution rules during menstruation and death in the family, and Kavitha complies, though she quietly finds some of it excessive. Diwali, Ugadi and Sankranti are the big festivals; the family visits the Yagachi dam for a picnic on Sankranti and the Shravanabelagola Gomateshwara during the Mahamastakabhisheka years, though the last one was 2018 and the next is not until 2030. Kavitha's social life centres on the anganwadi—her colleagues are her close friends, and they share meals, gossip and the small humiliations of government service. She is a member of a Stree Shakti self-help group organised under the SKDRDP model common in Hassan and Chikkamagaluru; the group saved ₹500 per member per month and accessed a bank-linkage loan two years ago, which Kavitha used to buy a refrigerator. The group meets fortnightly, and the collective strength—fifteen women, mostly Vokkaligas—gives her a voice she does not have alone.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Kavitha interacts with government most directly through her anganwadi job—her salary is paid by the Women and Child Development Department, often late, and she navigates a thicket of mobile apps, attendance registers and nutrition-stock reconciliations that consume hours each month. Her husband is a JD(S) supporter, loyal to the Gowda family legacy in Hassan and Holenarasipura, and they argue mildly about it; she cares less about party labels than about bus passes, school fees and hospital access. The Shakti scheme's free bus travel has been transformative—Kavitha now takes the bus to Hassan town for errands without calculating the fare, and Rakshitha uses it for tuition classes. She has never met her MLA but knows his name and his family's local clout. The gram panchayat repaired the anganwadi roof last year after her supervisor escalated a complaint, but a request for a compound wall has stalled. Kavitha's view of government is instrumental and unillusioned—it provides her salary, her mother-in-law's medicines and her children's subsidised schooling, but every entitlement requires paperwork, waiting and often a helpful intermediary.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Kavitha is proud of Belur—the Chennakeshava Temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site as of 2023, part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, and she tells visitors and her children that this is proof of Kannada civilisation's greatness. She worries constantly about money—the tractor loan, Rakshitha's future fees, Akash's weaker English, the cost of her mother-in-law's medicines, the possibility of a failed coconut harvest. She blames the government for low procurement prices and the middlemen who dominate the Arsikere coconut market, and she blames Manjunath mildly for not diversifying into something more profitable, though she knows he has little capital or risk appetite. She wants Rakshitha to have the education and independence she did not, to avoid early marriage and financial dependence, and she is fierce on this point, overruling her mother-in-law when necessary. She resents the double burden—full-time anganwadi work, part-time homestay work and all the household labour—and wishes Manjunath did more, though she rarely says so aloud. She fears illness, accident and the gap between her children's aspirations and their means; every private-school advertisement is a reminder of what she cannot afford. She takes satisfaction in her anganwadi work—she knows every child's name and history, and mothers thank her—but the pay is insultingly low for the responsibility. She sees Bengaluru as both opportunity and threat: the city could give Rakshitha a job, but it might also mean losing her to marriage outside the community or to a life Kavitha cannot imagine. She demands better schools, healthcare and fair prices, and she has stopped expecting politicians to deliver them without pressure.
